questions.prompt: A safelisted cross-origin POST reached the API and the browser blocked response access. What can have happened?

options.label: The server may already have changed state; inspect server evidence.
CORS automatically rolled the operation back.
A blocked response proves no request was sent.

questions.explanation: For this request shape, sending precedes the response-sharing check. CORS does not roll back server effects and an unreadable response cannot prove absence of mutation.

questions.prompt: A custom-header operation requires preflight and that preflight fails. What follows for the browser?

options.label: It does not send that guarded operation after this failed preflight.
It sends the operation anyway but hides only the response.
This proves all other request shapes are blocked.

questions.explanation: The failed required preflight prevents this operation. That differs from response blocking after a safelisted request, and does not establish behavior for other request shapes.

questions.prompt: An allowed-origin request has a valid session and CSRF proof but targets another user’s object. What must the server still do?

options.label: Check authorization for that actor, object and operation.
Trust the origin as proof that the actor owns the object.
Treat the CSRF token as permission to every object.

questions.explanation: Neither allowed response-sharing origin nor valid anti-forgery proof grants object access. Authentication identifies an actor; authorization checks the requested operation.

questions.prompt: When reviewing a cross-site session attack, what assumption must be checked?

options.label: Whether the browser’s actual cookie and request policies permit the credentials to be sent.
Cookies are always sent on every cross-site request.
Cookies can never be sent on cross-site requests.

questions.explanation: Cookie attributes, browser policies and request context affect credential sending. Both absolute claims erase assumptions required by a concrete trace.

questions.prompt: Revocation is recorded at time 10, but a sensitive API operation at 12 has only status cached at 0. The policy requires current status. What follows?

options.label: Refuse the sensitive operation until current status is established; record the propagation gap.
Trust the still-valid signature and ignore unknown session status.
A logout record proves every API has already enforced revocation.

questions.explanation: The exercise requires current status. Cached or unavailable evidence cannot establish it; cryptographic validity is a separate check.

questions.prompt: What identity should a denylist review require after token verification?

options.label: Use a unique server-issued identifier in the verified issuer/application scope; raw-token hashes may be bypassed.
Hash the serialized token and assume every valid representation has identical bytes.
Trust an unverified jti supplied by the caller as globally unique.

questions.explanation: Equivalent valid token representations can defeat a raw-byte key. Verify required claims and preserve issuer/application scope.

questions.prompt: A refresh token was revoked. What can you conclude about an already-issued access token?

options.label: Check the server’s cascade policy and consumer enforcement; revoking refresh access alone is not proof about issued access tokens.
Every access token in every consumer is necessarily invalid immediately.
Every issued access token necessarily remains valid until expiry regardless of server policy.

questions.explanation: RFC 7009 allows token/grant cascade policies and recognizes propagation. Inspect actual enforcement rather than either absolute.

questions.prompt: An API still trusts the old signing key after the issuer begins using a new key. Why can an old unexpired token still pass?

options.label: The verifier still trusts the old key; issuing a new key alone does not revoke that token.
Every verifier automatically rejects all old tokens whenever a new key is issued.
Key rotation selectively revokes only the user who logged out.

questions.explanation: Issuing keys and withdrawing consumer trust are different events; removing an old key has a broader affected-token scope.
